name: The Flickering Years: When Movies Had No Voice
description: From a Leeds garden in 1888 to the arrival of sound: the inventors, stars and studios of the silent film era, and the classics that survive.

checkpoints.name: Moving pictures appear
checkpoints.note: Roundhay Garden Scene, filmed in Leeds in 1888, is one of the earliest surviving films. Edison's company develops the Kinetoscope, which one viewer watches at a time, and in 1895 the Lumière brothers show Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory to a paying audience, followed by Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat.

checkpoints.name: Stories and studios
checkpoints.note: A Trip to the Moon (1902), by Georges Méliès, uses trick effects to tell a fantasy, and The Great Train Robbery (1903) tells a crime story with cuts between places. Silent film becomes a popular entertainment, and studios such as Paramount, founded in 1912, take shape.

checkpoints.name: Stars and shadows
checkpoints.note: Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford and Buster Keaton become stars known on every continent. German Expressionist films such as The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (made by Decla-Bioscop) and Nosferatu (made by Prana Film) play with shadow and fear, while UFA grows into Germany's leading studio. Warner Bros. and MGM join the Hollywood studios, and Battleship Potemkin (1925) shows the power of editing.

checkpoints.name: Sound arrives
checkpoints.note: Metropolis (1927) imagines a vast future city, and London After Midnight (1927) is now lost. The Jazz Singer (1927) brings sung and spoken words to a feature, and sound soon replaces silents. The first Academy Awards follow in 1929, Garbo first speaks on screen in 1930, and Chaplin's Modern Times (1936) is still mostly silent, with music, effects, a few machine voices and one nonsense song.
